conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me about the chest pain that brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. It’s that same left chest pain I’ve had before, but it’s worse now. It’s been constant for three weeks—sharp and worse when I press on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is it in the same spot as before, near your lower breastbone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right there. And it goes to my back. It hurts more when I eat, sit up, or take a deep breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any shortness of breath, sweating, or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No sweating or trouble breathing, but I’ve felt a bit lightheaded and haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll check your heart first to make sure nothing serious is going on. You had an EKG and chest X-ray in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will those tell you if it’s my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The EKG shows your heart rhythm is normal, and there are no signs of a heart attack. Your chest X-ray looks clear too—no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why does it hurt so much if it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is reproducible—meaning it flares when we press on it—which suggests it’s musculoskeletal. Given your history, this looks like a flare of your myofascial pain syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s muscle-related, like before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve had trigger point injections in the past for this. We’ll keep monitoring you and check your heart enzymes over the next few hours to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked your first set of blood tests. Your troponin level is less than 0.01—completely normal. That’s a good sign your heart isn’t damaged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Does that mean I’m not having a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it means we can rule that out. We’ll repeat the test tonight and tomorrow morning, but so far, everything points away from your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your second troponin came back normal again. Your heart rhythm has also been stable on the monitor overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident it’s not cardiac. Your pain pattern, normal tests, and history all support this being a flare-up of your chronic muscle pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood pressure? It was high in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 180 over 79. But that’s not unusual during pain or stress. We’ve kept you on your usual metoprolol, and it’s been better since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take that every day for my blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re continuing all your home meds: lasix for your heart, pantoprazole for your stomach, and ibuprofen for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the ibuprofen safe with my stomach medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because you’re on pantoprazole, which protects your stomach. We’re using it carefully and only for a short time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your third troponin is back—still normal. We’ve ruled out a heart issue completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll focus on managing the pain. Since it’s similar to past flares, your pain management team can help with trigger point injections soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before—they help a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll make sure you have a follow-up. For now, rest and take your meds as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still there, but not as intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re discharging you today since you’re stable and your heart has been ruled out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your medications. Weigh yourself every morning—call your doctor if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from my heart doctor. Any diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—stick to a 2-gram sodium diet and limit fluids to about 2 liters a day. It helps your heart and reduces swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I have my pain clinic appointment next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Call your primary doctor if the chest pain gets worse with shortness of breath, fever, or sweating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Your vein blood draw came back normal—no infections or issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that the blood test this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a routine check. Everything looks good. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is over. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. You’ll continue the same meds: furosemide, pantoprazole, ibuprofen, and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have all those at home. I’ll keep taking them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly as before. And keep that 2-gram sodium diet—no salty foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch what I eat. Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Rest up and follow up with your pain clinic. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re feeling stable, no new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, same pain but manageable. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. The transport team will take you out shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your discharge summary is ready. Diagnosis is acute flare of myofascial pain syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That matches what I’ve had before. I’ll manage it with my team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’ve listed your other conditions—high blood pressure and diastolic heart failure—for your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Thank you for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can I start by confirming your name?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's Margaret. I’ve been coughing for two weeks now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Margaret. I see you came in with a cough and some shortness of breath. Your daughter mentioned you also had a headache and body aches yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my muscles hurt, and I felt achy. But no fever. The cough is dry—no mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We did a chest X-ray in the ER, and it shows pneumonia in the lower part of your left lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we need to treat, but you’re already on antibiotics. You got azithromycin and levofloxacin in the ER, but we’re switching to ceftriaxone because of your allergy to levaquin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh yes, I can’t take levaquin—I had a bad reaction before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly, so we’re avoiding that. You’re on IV antibiotics now and will switch to oral ones later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m breathing a bit harder, but my chest pain hasn’t gotten worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your chronic left chest pain isn’t flaring up, which is reassuring. We’re watching your oxygen levels. Right now, you’re on 2 liters of oxygen through a nasal cannula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need oxygen the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not. Many patients improve within a day or two. We’ll check your oxygen when you walk and at rest to see when you can come off it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Margaret. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Cough is still there, but I’m not as short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your oxygen saturation is 94% on room air now—up from earlier. We’re going to try you off the oxygen and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s good news!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We also checked your blood work. Your white blood cell count was high, which confirms infection, but it’s responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I have diastolic heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart function is stable. Your ejection fraction is 65%, which is normal. We’re keeping you on your usual furosemide and metoprolol to manage your blood pressure and heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take 60 mg of furosemide at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re continuing that. We’re making sure you’re not dehydrated, especially since you were on oxygen. Staying hydrated helps your lungs clear the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Margaret, I just reviewed your morning labs. Your kidney function is normal, and your electrolytes are stable. That’s important with furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been drinking water and eating small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We want you to keep eating and drinking. That helps your body fight the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a little nausea, but no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted that. It could be from the antibiotics or the illness itself. We’ll keep an eye on it. Pantoprazole should help protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Margaret. You made it through the night without oxygen and your saturation stayed at 95% when walking. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Still a bit tired, but breathing is easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready to go home today. We’ll switch your IV antibiotics to oral ones—cefpodoxime and azithromycin—for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Same as the one I got in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Azithromycin is the same, but cefpodoxime is different from levofloxacin—safer for you. You’ll take two pills a day for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my other medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your regular medications. We’re adjusting your furosemide to 20 mg three times a day instead of 60 mg once. It’s the same total dose, but spread out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. And metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one 25 mg sustained-release tablet daily. Same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to follow a low-salt diet, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2 grams of sodium a day. And weigh yourself every morning. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember from last time. And see my primary doctor soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Follow up in a week. If your cough worsens or you run a fever, call sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’re discharging you home. Your daughter will help you get settled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s waiting outside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Keep resting, take your meds, and call if anything changes. You’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How’s your breathing now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still good. Cough is less frequent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oxygen is 95% on room air while walking—perfect. We’ll finalize your discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the nurse go over your medications one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Margaret, your discharge is approved. The nurse will bring your prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll make sure I understand the doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. And remember—call if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Margaret. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___ . I’m Dr. ___ . You’re here because of chest pain and shortness of breath. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My chest pain on the left side has been worse for five days. It’s a burning, tight feeling. And I’ve been struggling to catch my breath, especially when I move or take a deep breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any cough, fever, or palpitations?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a dry cough and felt feverish. Also, my heart has been racing sometimes, and I’ve felt dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We did a CT scan of your chest in the ER, and it showed blood clots in both lungs—what we call pulmonary emboli. That’s likely why you’re having these symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blood clots in my lungs? That sounds serious. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but we’ve started treatment. You’re on a blood thinner through your IV called heparin, and you’re getting oxygen to help you breathe easier. We’ll switch to other medications soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had clots before in my leg. Is this related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history of DVT—deep vein thrombosis—puts you at higher risk. We think that’s what led to these clots in your lungs. We’ll keep you on blood thinners to prevent more clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my chest pain and headache? They’ve been bad for a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know you’ve had chronic left-sided chest pain and headaches. The chest pain may feel worse now because of the clots. We’re giving you acetaminophen with codeine for pain, and we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also take ibuprofen at home. Can I keep using that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can use ibuprofen if needed, but we’re being cautious because of your kidney function. We noticed your creatinine went up a bit, so we’re watching your kidneys closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys? What happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine rose to 1.3, up from your usual 0.7 or 0.8. This may be from the contrast dye used in the CT scan or from mild dehydration. We’ve given you IV fluids, and your levels are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. So it’s getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last lab showed creatinine back down to 0.7. That’s a good sign. We’ll keep checking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my heart? I have heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your beta blocker for heart failure. Your furosemide was paused because of the kidney issue, but we’ll restart it once we’re sure your kidneys are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood pressure medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on metoprolol. We’re keeping your blood pressure well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. My breathing isn’t as bad, but I still need the oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ve switched you from heparin to a medication called Lovenox, which you’ll get as a shot twice a day. You’ll also start Coumadin, a pill that works over days to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of Coumadin. I need blood tests for that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We checked your INR today—it’s 1.7. We want it above 2. Until then, you’ll keep taking Lovenox along with Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll go home with both?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with Lovenox shots for five more days and Coumadin. You’ll need a blood test soon after discharge to check your INR and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who do I send the results to?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To Dr. ___. The lab will fax them directly. He’ll adjust your Coumadin dose based on the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxygen? Do I need that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home with oxygen at 2 liters. It’s a precaution while your lungs recover. We’ll reassess in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your INR is stable, and your kidneys are back to normal. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lovenox shots twice daily for five days and take Coumadin as prescribed. Resume your usual medications, including furosemide, ibuprofen as needed, and your stomach protector, pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can use acetaminophen-codeine as needed for pain, and ibuprofen if that’s not enough. But avoid NSAIDs if you feel unwell or have stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have worsening chest pain, trouble breathing, fever, or swelling in your legs, call your doctor or go to the ER right away. These could be signs of another clot or complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your home health team follows up. Take care, and follow those instructions closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your granddaughter can help you with the Lovenox shots if needed. The nurse will show her how before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s been helping me. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to be going home, but I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right approach. Recovery takes time, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get the blood test done right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. That’s very important for adjusting your Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up, and Dr. ___ will manage your anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well, and we’ll get you home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will review your medications and oxygen setup before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll listen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We want to make sure you’re safe and informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I understand you’ve been having chest pain that radiates to your abdomen and back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago. It’s worse in the morning. Feels like burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also had some shortness of breath, nausea, and dizziness. We checked your blood and found your hemoglobin is low—only 7.8—and your INR is too high at 4.3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low blood? And INR? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood count is low, which means you may have lost blood somewhere. The INR measures how thin your blood is. Since you’re on warfarin, a high INR increases bleeding risk. We’ll adjust your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. I’ve been on that for my blood clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know. We also did a CT scan to check for serious causes. It showed a small ulcer in the aorta in your belly—called an infrarenal aortic ulceration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aorta? That sounds serious. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and stable. The vascular team says no surgery is needed now. But we must control your blood pressure and fix your INR to prevent any risk of bleeding or rupture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand. What about the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG and heart enzymes were normal, so it’s likely not your heart. Given your history of chest wall pain and past relief from injections, we think it’s musculoskeletal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your oxygen level dropped a bit yesterday. The chest X-ray showed some atelectasis—part of the lung is collapsed. We think it’s due to shallow breathing, maybe from pain or heart strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Collapsed lung? Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild. We gave you a diuretic—lasix—to reduce fluid from your heart. You’re doing better, but you still drop oxygen when you walk. We may send you home with oxygen for activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need oxygen at home? Just when I walk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just with exertion. We’ll monitor it. Also, your stool tested positive for blood, so we need to find where you’re losing blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had stomach pain too. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re scheduling an endoscopy and colonoscopy to check your stomach and colon. You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. Will I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because your hemoglobin is very low. We’ll give you two units of red blood cells to help you feel stronger and prevent strain on your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just checking in. Your blood counts are stable after the transfusion. We’re still waiting for the endoscopy and colonoscopy tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My stomach still hurts sometimes. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and constipation could be making it worse. We’ve added a stool softener. The procedures will help us see if there’s gastritis or diverticulosis—common causes of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of diverticulosis. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. It’s small pouches in the colon. They can bleed, especially with a high INR. We’ll manage it with diet and iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you did well with the endoscopy and colonoscopy today. We found gastritis and diverticulosis, but no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bleeding? Then why is my blood low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We think you had a small bleed from one of those areas, but it stopped. The high INR made it more likely. Now that we’ve corrected it, the risk is lower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Your hemoglobin stayed stable after the transfusion. We’re starting you on iron pills to rebuild your blood over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them. What about my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We lowered your dose to 2 mg daily. You’ll need to follow up with your doctor to check your INR regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the aortic ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still no surgery needed. Just keep your blood pressure under control and stay on the adjusted warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. Hemoglobin is holding, INR is now in range. You’re moving better, but still desaturate a little with walking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll go home with oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just 2 liters when you’re active. It’s a precaution. Your heart and lungs are stable, but we want to support you as you recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach? Should I change my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, eat more fiber—fruits, vegetables, whole grains. It helps with diverticulosis and constipation. Keep taking the pantoprazole for your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using heat on my skin for pain. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed the blisters. They’re likely from the heat therapy. Be careful—your skin can burn easily. Let’s focus on safer pain relief like acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll stop that. My neck and feet still hurt sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing that with Tylenol. It’s likely from arthritis and myofascial pain, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day—we’re discharging you. You’re stable, hemoglobin is good, and your pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your medications: warfarin daily, metoprolol twice a day, furosemide, pantoprazole, iron, and stool softener. Use oxygen with activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your primary doctor soon to check your INR and iron levels. Call if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my grandson will help me at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s perfect. He can help with meds and watching for any changes. We’re sending services to check on you too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge papers ready. Rest well, eat healthy, and take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep up with your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. We’re glad to see you improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m grateful for all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is here for you. Take care and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay healthy and out of the hospital!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. We’ll get your discharge orders finalized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’re all set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having stomach pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had pain in my upper belly for about three weeks. Last night I threw up, but it wasn’t bloody. This morning I had dark, sticky stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. Dark stool can mean there’s bleeding in the upper part of your digestive tract. We also saw your blood count is very low—your hemoglobin is only 5.9, and your INR is dangerously high at 11.6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: INR? I take Coumadin for my blood clots. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your INR measures how thin your blood is. Normal is around 2–3, but yours is over 11, which means you’re at high risk for bleeding. We’ve given you vitamin K and started blood products to reverse that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know it was that high. I’ve also been taking Advil for my chest and back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely part of the problem. Advil and other NSAIDs can irritate the stomach lining, especially when combined with a high INR. We’ve stopped both Coumadin and Advil for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay? I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking good care of you. You’ve already received fluids, vitamin K, and one unit of blood. We’re giving more blood and clotting factors to stabilize you. You’re in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan of the head showed no bleeding, which is great news. Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in the lungs, related to your heart condition, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart is enlarged, and there’s fluid buildup—what we call congestive heart failure. It’s been worse lately, probably because of the anemia. Once your blood count improves, your breathing should too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood test shows your hemoglobin is improving—from 5.9 to 6.3. Your INR is coming down too, from 11.6 to 41, thanks to the vitamin K.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re still concerned. Your stomach is tender, and you passed another dark stool. We’ve consulted GI—they recommend an endoscopy tomorrow to look for the source of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ll have your endoscopy today. It’s a procedure where a camera goes through your mouth to look at your esophagus, stomach, and upper intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you’ll sleep through it. It’s very safe. We need to find where the bleeding is coming from and make sure there’s no active ulcer or tear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy is done. You have esophagitis and gastritis—irritation in your esophagus and stomach—but no active bleeding or ulcers. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, it’s from the combination of Advil and your high INR. The irritation from the Advil, plus your blood being too thin, led to the bleed. We’ll keep you on a strong stomach medicine—omeprazole—twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t take Advil anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll also test for H. pylori, a bacteria that can cause stomach inflammation. Your blood test came back positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can that be treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with antibiotics. We’ll let your primary doctor know so they can start the treatment after you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is now 7.2 and your INR is 2.8—much better. You’ve stopped having black stools, which means the bleeding has likely stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from the anemia. You’ve received five units of blood, and your body needs time to adjust. We’ve restarted your diuretic—lasix—to help with the fluid in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 20 mg at home. Now it’s 40 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because your breathing was worse. We also gave IV lasix. Your oxygen levels are better now—94% on room air when resting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the fluid in your lungs is still there but stable. We’ll keep you on lasix and monitor your weight and breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My chest pain is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your heart—it’s not a heart attack. Your pain is musculoskeletal, likely from old injuries. We’ll keep using lidocaine patches and Percocet as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a colonoscopy today. Even though the upper GI bleed seems under control, we want to check your colon for other sources.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s important. You have diverticulosis—small pouches in the colon—which can sometimes bleed. We just want to make sure nothing’s active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy is done. You have diverticula, but no active bleeding or signs of ischemia. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So everything’s okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. Your heart failure is improving, your bleeding has stopped, and we’ve found no new issues. We’re just waiting for one more blood test and to make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is now 8.1 and your INR is 1.8. You’re doing well. We’re planning to restart your Coumadin tomorrow at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was scared to start it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you need it to prevent blood clots. We’ll start low and monitor closely. Your ultrasound showed no new clots in your legs, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I fell last night. I was getting up to go to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I heard. You hit your left wrist and right knee. No one saw you pass out, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I just tripped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get X-rays to make sure there’s no fracture. In the meantime, orthopedics will see you and likely give you a splint and a walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your X-rays show no fractures. Just arthritis and old changes. But you do need to be more careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They gave me a splint and a walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you must use the walker at all times. Your balance is weak, and another fall could be serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your breathing is stable, your blood counts are improving, and you’re not bleeding anymore. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, take all your medications as prescribed. Your metoprolol is now 25 mg once a day instead of 50 mg. Your lasix is 40 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the omeprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a day for now. No NSAIDs—no Advil, Aleve, or aspirin. Use acetaminophen if you need pain relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 2 mg at bedtime. Follow up with the anticoagulation clinic to check your INR regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the lidocaine patches and Percocet as needed. But if the pain changes—gets worse or spreads—go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable. Remember: weigh yourself daily, limit salt, use your walker, and keep all follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. If you vomit blood, have black stools, trouble breathing, or chest pain, go to the ER right away. Otherwise, see your doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your daughter will help you at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s picking me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And home health will send a nurse to check on you. Take it slow, and don’t rush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll see you in follow-up, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson about Advil.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart move. Your stomach and your blood thinner don’t mix well with NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to the meds you gave me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And call if anything changes. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.text: Yes, the headache’s been worse than usual. I’ve had it for a while, but it got really bad yesterday.

conversation_lines.text: Oh. I did see a little blood on the toilet paper, but I didn’t know how long that’s been happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll have an upper endoscopy and a colonoscopy to look for the source of bleeding. The GI team will be involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that what caused the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be part of it. We also did a colonoscopy. You have diverticulosis—small pouches in the colon—but no active bleeding there either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So where’s the blood coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling short of breath too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen level was low—88% on room air. Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in the lungs, likely from your heart condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have heart failure, yes. I take Lasix for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We gave you a dose of IV Lasix yesterday, and we’re restarting your oral diuretic. That should help with the breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my headache? It’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a head CT, and there’s no bleeding or stroke. Your headache may be related to your blood pressure or anemia. It should improve as we treat those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat chest X-ray shows improvement in the lung fluid. Your oxygen levels are better—95% on two liters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel less winded. What about my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram. Your heart’s pumping function is okay—ejection fraction is 55%—but there’s some worsening of mitral regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we need to stay on top of your heart failure. We’ll keep you on Lasix and restart your metoprolol, which helps your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they stopped it when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we held it temporarily because your blood pressure was low. Now that you’re more stable, it’s safe to restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin has stabilized at 8.1. That’s good progress after the transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not losing more blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tested positive for blood, but your levels aren’t dropping, so it’s likely a slow, small bleed. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed it with your son. Since you’re stable and no active bleed was found, we won’t do another one now. The GI team doesn’t recommend a capsule study either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 1.8, which is in a safer range. We’re going to restart your Coumadin tonight at the same dose—2 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But won’t that increase my risk of bleeding again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a balance. You have a history of blood clots—PE and DVT—so stopping it completely isn’t safe. We’ll monitor your INR closely after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also keeping you on Prilosec twice a day to protect your stomach. No NSAIDs, just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my chest pain? It flared up again last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and troponins—no sign of a heart attack. It’s likely your usual musculoskeletal pain. We’ve restarted your tramadol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your headache has also improved, which is great. No new imaging needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications: Coumadin at bedtime, Prilosec daily, Lasix, metoprolol, and tramadol as needed. You’ll also have home health services to check on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor soon to check your INR and review your meds. Also follow up with GI as recommended. Call if you see black stools or feel dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I use the albuterol inhaler?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you have shortness of breath or wheezing. It’s a rescue inhaler, so keep it handy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my walker—I’ll need that for stability?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your hip replacement and balance. Use it to stay safe at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any other questions before we finalize discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think that covers everything. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’ve had this burning pain on the left side of my chest again. It started last night and didn’t go away. It goes down my arm and into my jaw too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Does it get worse when you take a deep breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it does. And I felt nauseous too. I tried my diclofenac gel and some Tylenol, but nothing helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You’ve had this kind of pain before, right? Your son mentioned it happens a few times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been going on for years. But it’s always sharp and in the same spot. Never during activity, only at rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We did an EKG in the ER, and it didn’t show any signs of a heart attack. Your cardiac enzymes are also normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? I was really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t look like it’s coming from your heart. We also did a CT scan of your chest to check for blood clots, and that was clear too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. But why does it hurt so much then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When I examined you, I noticed the area over your left rib is very tender. That, along with the fact that the pain worsens with breathing, makes us think this is costochondritis—arthritis of the chest wall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve heard of that. But why now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can flare up for various reasons. We also noticed you have some numbness in your left arm. Has that been happening too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sometimes. It comes and goes. My grandson says it might be from my neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. You have cervical spine arthritis, which can cause nerve irritation and lead to arm numbness. It’s probably not related to your chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But I’ve been feeling tired lately. Could that be from something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we found that your blood count is low. Your hemoglobin was 8.3, which explains the fatigue. This is called anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anemia? I had that before. Is it from my stomach bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your stool tested positive for a small amount of blood. Given your history of gastritis and being on blood thinners, this is likely a slow, chronic bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do take Coumadin for my blood clots. Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re keeping you on it. You’ve had serious clots before, and stopping it could be dangerous. But we are adjusting your stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take Prilosec sometimes, but not every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your grandson mentioned you’ve also been taking naproxen for the pain. That’s a problem—it can worsen stomach bleeding, especially with Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know it was dangerous. I just wanted relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re stopping all NSAIDs—no ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin unless we prescribe it. You should only use Tylenol for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll stop those. What else should I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your omeprazole to 40 mg twice a day to protect your stomach. We’re also starting an iron supplement to help your blood count improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Iron? Like ferrous sulfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet daily. And we’ll refer you to gastroenterology for a repeat endoscopy to check your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The Tylenol every few hours is helping. Still a bit sore when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Your latest blood test shows your hematocrit is stable at 28.4%, which is near your baseline. No further drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re stable. Your heart failure is also under control—you’re not retaining fluid, and your breathing is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about my heart again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re doing well—pain is controlled, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the new omeprazole dose twice daily, take the iron every day, and stick to Tylenol for pain. No NSAIDs. Use your Voltaren gel if needed, but not too often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking it as directed. Your dose is adjusted—three 1mg tablets on Fridays, and one 2mg tablet the other days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary doctor in a week, and gastroenterology will call to schedule your endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if the pain worsens or if you notice black stools or vomiting blood. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. You’re here because of some elbow pain and low blood counts. Can you tell me about the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… left elbow. Started suddenly. No injury. Goes down to hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, swelling, or redness in the elbow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just pain when I move it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also noticed your blood count is very low—your hemoglobin is 5.4. That’s why you might feel more tired than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I feel okay… son says I’ve been better lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. But your stool tested positive for blood, and you’re on warfarin, which thins the blood. Your INR is 6.0—much higher than it should be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Warfarin for clots. I know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because of the high INR and low blood count, we’re giving you vitamin K to reverse the warfarin and will likely give you blood transfusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Transfusion? Is it bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but treatable. The bleeding is likely from your stomach or intestines. You’ve had this before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… black stools. But I take iron. Always dark.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. But the black color can also mean bleeding. We’ll monitor you closely. We’ve started the vitamin K, and you’ll get blood slowly over the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your hemoglobin improved to 28.5 after two units of blood. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Elbow feels less painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The elbow pain is improving on its own. X-rays were normal, so no fracture or joint issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But I had trouble breathing last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen dipped to 90%. We think it’s because you got some fluid from the transfusion and your heart is a bit overloaded. We gave you Lasix to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heart? I have CHF.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s well-managed. But with the extra fluid, it got a little stressed. We’ll keep an eye on your breathing and weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your H. pylori test back—it’s positive. But your doctor said you were treated for it last year, so we won’t repeat treatment now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. Antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue your pantoprazole to protect your stomach. The GI team will see you soon to talk about long-term prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve had two more units of blood. Your hemoglobin is stable. No more bleeding from the stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to make sure your INR comes down and you’re not at risk for more bleeding. We reversed it with vitamin K and FFP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it for now. Your doctor prefers to restart it, but we need to discuss the risks—bleeding again vs. risk of clots if you stop it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want clots. Had PEs before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’ll restart your usual dose, but your son should call the clinic if you eat less than usual—poor intake can raise your INR again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: He will. I eat less when I’m not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll check your INR soon and again after discharge. Also, weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than 3 pounds, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.4—much better. We’re going to restart your warfarin tonight at your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my heart medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your metoprolol for a bit, but we’ll restart it. Your blood pressure is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. Your hemoglobin is stable, no more bleeding, and your INR is in a safer range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your medications as listed: warfarin, pantoprazole, furosemide, and acetaminophen for pain. No NSAIDs, even topical, on your chest—switch to acetaminophen gel if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. CBC and INR check on the scheduled date. Call if you feel weak, dizzy, or have black stools. And weigh yourself daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Your son will help you at home, and home health will check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. He’s very helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should feel more energy now that your blood count is up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already do. Much better than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we wanted to hear. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… it started about a week ago. First in the middle, then spread everywhere. Worse on the lower left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the pain constant? Does anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s always there. Doesn’t change with eating. I’ve also felt sick to my stomach and threw up a few times—nothing came out, just clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, diarrhea, or recent travel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No diarrhea—I haven’t gone in a few days. Haven’t gone anywhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see you were on pantoprazole for heartburn. Are you still taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No… ran out two weeks ago. Prescription expired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll restart that. Your CT scan showed some inflammation in a small part of your bowel—likely enteritis, an infection or irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be uncomfortable, but we’re treating it. You’re already on two antibiotics—Bactrim and Flagyl—because you’re allergic to Levaquin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh yes, I can’t take that one. Makes me very sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly, so we chose safe alternatives. We also found signs of a urinary tract infection. That’s being treated with the same Bactrim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel like I had a UTI… no burning or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes in older adults, UTIs don’t cause the usual symptoms. The urine test showed infection, so we’re treating it just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work shows your hemoglobin is low—9.4, down from before. But it’s stable. No active bleeding signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was here for bleeding… I got transfusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but this time, no transfusion is needed. Your levels are low but not critical. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I have CHF.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart function is still preserved. The chest X-ray shows mild enlargement and a little fluid, but you’re breathing fine. We’re keeping you on your usual furosemide and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to get swollen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that. Now, your warfarin—we’ve lowered it to 1 mg daily while you’re on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why? I don’t want another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly why we’re not stopping it. But antibiotics can make warfarin stronger, raising bleeding risk. So we lower the dose temporarily and check your INR regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand. When will I feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should start feeling improvement in a day or two. The antibiotics are working. We’ll keep you hydrated and manage nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still sore, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Your repeat labs show white blood cells are normalizing. The stool test came back—no C. diff, no Salmonella or Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not food poisoning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. It’s more likely a bacterial enteritis not from those common causes. The antibiotics are covering it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the urine infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine culture shows a gram-negative rod—likely E. coli. Bactrim covers that. We’ll finish the course and you’ll be fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my potassium was low yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 3.0, so we gave IV potassium. This morning it’s 3.7—back to normal. You’re also on oral pantoprazole again to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I forgot to refill it… won’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your symptoms have improved enough that we can discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish both antibiotics—Bactrim twice daily and Flagyl three times daily for four more days. Continue pantoprazole daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on 1 mg daily for now. Your clinic will check your INR soon and adjust it back when safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my water pill? I take 60 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing it to 20 mg three times a day—so 60 mg total—but spread out. Helps with swelling without dropping your pressure too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And if my belly pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. But you’re on the mend. Also, drink plenty of fluids and take docusate if constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. A nurse will go over your prescriptions, and you’ll have follow-up with your primary doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my grandson will help me at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll make sure he knows how to help. Take care, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having some pain when swallowing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it felt like a burning from my mouth down to my chest. It started after I ate beans—gave me heartburn, I think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you vomit? Any nausea or stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did throw up, but no stomach pain. The burning was the worst part. It got better after they gave me something in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you received IV pantoprazole and a GI cocktail, which helps calm stomach acid. Your EKG was normal, so we’re not concerned about a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. But they said something about my oxygen being low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen level dropped to 91% for a short time, even though you weren’t short of breath. The chest X-ray showed mild fluid in the lungs, likely from your heart condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, my heart failure? I’ve had that for years. EF is around 55%, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You have diastolic heart failure, and the fluid buildup is mild. We gave you a dose of Lasix in the ER to help clear it. Your oxygen is now 94% on room air—much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll need more Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your usual dose—20 mg daily. No need for extra now. But you should weigh yourself every morning. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heartburn—will that come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep taking pantoprazole 40 mg daily. If you feel heartburn again, you can take Tums as needed. They’re over the counter. Also, follow up with your gastroenterologist—might need another endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood work? I remember being anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low but stable—around 6.9. It’s chronic microcytic anemia, likely from past GI bleeds. No signs of active bleeding now. Keep taking your iron pill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I take 2 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was a bit high when you arrived, so we held the dose last night. You can restart 2 mg tonight. Make sure to get your INR checked soon after discharge—your son has the lab order.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just one thing—your urine showed bacteria, but you have no symptoms. We’re waiting on a culture. If it grows something significant, your doctor might start antibiotics later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No symptoms, so no treatment now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We don’t treat asymptomatic bacteria unless there’s a high risk. We’ll let your PCP decide based on the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
